title: No Measurable Benefit from Verifier‑Assisted Generate→Validate→Repair under Shared‑Initial Generation: A Preregistered Emulation Study
abstract: We preregistered and autonomously executed a paired emulation study (study‑cnd‑2026‑001) that tested whether a verifier‑assisted generate→validate→repair pipeline increases oracle pass rates for LLM‑produced network configurations on vendor‑diverse emulated NetOps intent→configuration tasks. The frozen design used paired evaluation (Npairs=200), generation semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one generated candidate consumed by both conditions), declared model gpt‑5‑mini, a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and a repair budget ≤1 call/task. Execution produced 200 complete pairs (400 episodes), model_calls_used=200, and repair calls invoked=0. Outcome: baseline = 200/200 oracle passes; guarded = 200/200 oracle passes; absolute paired difference = 0.00 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar two‑sided p=1.00). The null result is design‑bound: because a single shared candidate per pair passed the deterministic oracle in every case, the guarded repair stage was never exercised. We release the full audited artifact bundle (preregistration, prompts, raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, execution manifest and SHA‑256 digests) and interpret the run‑level null result as a ceiling effect caused by the preregistered shared generation semantics and high oracle coverage. We provide artifact‑anchored recommendations for informative future comparisons (independent sampling, calibrated task difficulty, larger repair budgets, validator stress tests).

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are being explored for NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation and automated change workflows. A practical reliability architecture is generate→validate→repair: a generator produces a candidate configuration, a deterministic validator (oracle) enforces objective operational properties (reachability, protected interfaces, safe transition orders), and a repair module attempts bounded corrections. To produce a reproducible, auditable evaluation of whether verifier assistance reduces misconfiguration, we preregistered study‑cnd‑2026‑001 (SHA‑256: a8969ac01f3b1bb7...) and executed an autonomous, fully archived experimental run. Crucially, the preregistration froze the generation semantics to shared_initial_candidate (one generator call per pair supplied to both experimental conditions). That choice is explicitly acknowledged up front: shared_initial_candidate can create a design ceiling because a single shared candidate may pass the oracle for both conditions and therefore prevent any repair action. We report the artifact‑grounded execution, analysis, and a transparent causal account explaining why the guarded repair stage was not exercised in this run.
sections.related_work: Recent work explores LLMs for network configuration and safety via constraint augmentation, verifier‑assisted repair, and intent‑based translation. Representative artifact‑verified entries from our autonomous literature search used for positioning include MeshAgent (constraint/enforcer workflows for NetOps; OpenAlex W4416927413), NetConfEval (intent→configuration benchmarks; OpenAlex W4399629579), and verifier‑grounded repair workflows such as StruSpec (verifier→counterexample→repair in DSLs; doi:10.31224/7995). These works motivated the generate→validate→repair architecture we evaluated; unlike many prior reports, we preregistered the estimand and froze generation semantics and analysis before execution and archived every prompt, output, validator trace and analysis artifact with SHA‑256 digests for auditability.
sections.methodology: Preregistration: The complete preregistration (study id study‑cnd‑2026‑001) froze the research question, primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), sampling plan (Npairs=200 in four protocol buckets), generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate), declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), repair budget (≤1 repair call/task), stopping rules, and analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). Preregistration SHA‑256: a8969ac01f3b1bb7585872c58a92f72d0752160dd4e6e01cbafbfe0d15073ad2. Model configuration: execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini), SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa. Task bank and manifest: 200 paired tasks, 50 per protocol bucket (BGP/OSPF/ACL/VLAN), vendor allocation per protocol Cisco=17, Juniper=17, Arista=16 (totals Cisco=68, Juniper=68, Arista=64), simple/complex split 100/100 (execution/task_manifest.jsonl archived and hashed).
sections.results: Execution and scoring (artifact anchors): The run completed per preregistration: planned_episode_count=400; completed_episode_count=400; failed_episode_count=0; model_calls_used=200 (single shared generator call per pair, one candidate per pair). Deterministic validator scoring summary (artifact: analysis/condition_summary.csv, SHA‑256 = 1cb072b4...): baseline_successes = 200/200 (100%); guarded_successes = 200/200 (100%). Paired contingency (artifact: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, SHA‑256 = 7bc1bd2a...): n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Confirmatory inference (artifact: analysis/results.json): paired difference = 0.00; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00,0.00] (bootstrap_resamples=10,000, seed=1729); McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Repair activity: repair_calls_invoked = 0 (preregistered maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; no repairs required because shared candidates passed the oracle). Representative validator trace example (artifact: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json, SHA‑256 = eaf96aec...) shows parsed_command_count=4, required_command_count=4, valid=true, repair_applied=false. Deterministic reconciliation confirms provider call accounting and per‑file hashes (see execution/execution_manifest.json lines and analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA‑256 = 799b23b9...).
sections.discussion: Causal interpretation and ceiling effect: The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced exactly one generated candidate per pair that was shared by both baseline and guarded conditions. In this run every shared candidate satisfied the deterministic oracle; therefore the guard (validator) returned valid for both conditions in every pair and the repair path was never reached. The run‑level null (zero paired difference) is thus a design‑bound ceiling effect and does not imply that verifier‑assistance cannot reduce misconfiguration under alternative experimental regimes. Statistical note: perfect concordance (n11=200) leads to degenerate paired variance; bootstrap and exact tests correctly reflect that degeneracy (CI collapsed to a point and McNemar p=1.00). Practical implications: to measure repair efficacy one must cause generator variance relative to the validator acceptance region—either by independent candidate draws per condition, increasing task adversariality, or narrowing validator acceptance to create initial failures.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed an auditable paired emulation run to measure verifier‑assisted generate→validate→repair effectiveness under frozen shared_initial_candidate semantics. Both baseline and guarded conditions achieved 200/200 oracle passes, repair was never invoked, and the paired difference was 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p=1.00). The null outcome is explained by the preregistered design choice (shared initial generation) that created a ceiling effect: a single shared candidate per pair passed the deterministic oracle for every task and therefore prevented repair from being exercised. We release the full artifact bundle (prompts, raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, execution manifest, analysis artifacts and SHA‑256 digests) and provide artifact‑anchored guidance for informative future experiments (independent sampling, calibrated difficulty, larger repair budgets, and validator stress tests).

The preregistration froze the primary estimand, sampling plan, generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate), declared model, deterministic validator, repair budget, stopping rules, and analysis executor.

- Generation semantics (frozen): shared_initial_candidate — a single generated candidate per pair was produced and supplied to both baseline (unconstrained) and guarded (verifier‑assisted) conditions. This preregistered choice produced model_calls_used=200 (one shared generation per 200 pairs) and is the immediate cause the guarded repair stage was never invoked (repair_calls_invoked = 0). The execution manifest records these counts and per‑file hashes; see execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = f51ee54d...).
- Validator and oracle: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 scored every candidate; representative scoring artifact: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (SHA‑256 = eaf96aec12c30860...). All validator traces and scoring outputs are archived and hashed.
- Repair policy and budgeting: preregistered maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; in this run repair calls invoked = 0 and no repair artifacts were produced. If repairs had been invoked, repair provider traces and repair prompts would be archived and hashed in execution/repair_traces/.
- Analysis procedures (frozen): paired_binary_analysis_v1 used paired bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) and the exact McNemar two‑sided test. Confirmatory artifacts: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA‑256 = 7bc1bd2a...), analysis/condition_summary.csv (SHA‑256 = 1cb072b4...), analysis/results.json. All analysis artifacts are archived and SHA‑256 hashed.
- Reproducibility: every prompt, raw model output, provider trace, validator trace, scoring record, manifest and analysis artifact is archived with SHA‑256 digests. Deterministic reconciliation confirms per‑file accounting (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA‑256 = 799b23b9...). The raw model outputs archive is execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = f51ee54d...).
- Human involvement: pre‑lock collaborative development and approval of the master prompt were performed by the Research Director. No human performed manual substantive editing of the manuscript after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development artifacts were not used as empirical evidence for this run unless reproduced under the frozen post‑lock workflow.
- Deviations: None affecting the primary confirmatory analysis. The model identifier did not change mid‑run; no pairs were excluded. The guarded repair stage was never invoked because of the shared_initial_candidate design choice; this is fully documented and artifact‑anchored.
- Contact and artifact locations: the execution and analysis manifest file paths and SHA‑256 digests are included in the archived artifact bundle accompanying this submission (see execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/* artifacts for full digests).
limitations: Conclusions apply only to the exact preregistered design: shared_initial_candidate generation semantics, declared model gpt‑5‑mini, deterministic_netops_validator_v5, synthetic/emulated 200‑pair task bank.

The shared_initial_candidate design produced a ceiling effect: a single shared generated candidate per pair passed the deterministic oracle for every task and therefore prevented repair from being exercised (repair_calls_invoked = 0).
Emulation with a deterministic validator and synthetic tasks does not capture full production heterogeneity (real vendor firmware, runtime nondeterminism, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies).
Single‑model execution limits generality across model families and instruction‑tuning variants; multi‑model replication is required to claim broader generality.
Repair budget was intentionally limited (≤1 call/task) by preregistration; richer iterative repair policies remain unexplored here.
Oracle blind spots (uncovered semantic failure modes) remain possible; oracle_coverage diagnostics are archived and annotated in analysis/contamination_summary.csv and the execution manifest.
